2. GENERAL DESCRIPTION
2.1 The cup type ( with the axis of rotation normal to the flow) current meter comprises the bucket wheel and spindle bearings, the contact box housing the contact breaker, the yoke or main frame, ancl the tail fill, the details of which arc covered under IS: 3910-1966*.

3. ASSEMBLY AND ADJUSTMENT OF THE CURRENT METER 3.1 The current meter assembly sI1(:\11 comprise the tail unit consisting
of four fins which shall IJe secured to tile rear of the cradle casting by a taper pill. The lower of the tail fins carrying an adjustable courrterweight shall be set so tha t the meter stands hor izonta lly when sUSIJeJlded in water. The bucket wheel shall be clamped to the ver tical spindle by a hexagonal nut. The pivot holder should be examined to ensure that the pivot point is not damaged. TIle cap of the contact box SI1()111d be removed and the upper spindle bearing cleaned with a finely pointed piece of stick wrapped in clean rag. The bucket wheel assernbled with tile spindle shall be then placed in proper position, the pivot holder should be then passed through the lower boss eJ1SUI ~llg that tile raising handle ( or device) is ill ra ised position ancl the lower portion of the spindle shal! be secured to it with tile help of the clamping screw. The pivot holder itself shall be clamped securely to the cradle with the help of clamping screw. TIle contact box shall be placed through the upper boss and secured to tile ullper portion of the spindle in the cradle through the clamping screw. Before tightening the contact box to tile cradle, it should be ensured that the pill ill tile upper portion of the spindle is deflecting the contact spr ing at every rotation.

3.1.1 After tile current meter is assembled as above, it sha ll be subjected to various tests enumerated in 10.

4. GENERAL ACCESSORIES REQUIRED 4.1 Stop Watch - A good stop watch shall be provided at each site. It
should run for 30 minutes. It should be capable of being started, stopped and re-set to zero by consecutively pressing the Ileac} of the watch. It should work only when required and S}lOW the time correct to I/Sth of a second.

7.1 State 01 Flow - Current meters are rated in a rating tank where
turbulence, eddies, swirls and similar disturbances, are absent. It is, therefore, advisable to avoid observations where excessive turbulence occurs and where cross currents, swirls, eddies and similar disturbances and agitation of water are met with.

7.2 Angle of Current - A measuring cross-section of a stream shall be
so chosen that the flow is reasonably normal to the section. Deviation from the true normal may, however, occur at some observation points especially in wide and turbulent streams. To obtain accurate discharge measurement, this inclination shall be taken into consideration and the velocity component normal to the section computed and used ill discharge calculations, Horizontal angle may be measured by means of sextant, using a wooden float attached to a cotton cord when velocities are being observed at the surface, "Vhen cable suspension is used, care shall be taken to ensure that there is no tortional effect which would prevent current meter to direct itself along tile flow direction.
NOTE _. Other convenient instruments that 118VO been recently brought out are � pendulum current meter � devised at Dolft laboratory 811d the � direct reading current meter � brought out fly Kelvin Hughes.

7.3 Effect or Wind -l'hc wind may affect current meter observation in several ways. If observations arc made from a cable car or from a suspension bridge, the wind may cause these structures to oscillate, causing the current meter to swing inside water. If a boat is used, it rna}' heave due to waves. Besides disturbance so caused, the wind action may cause considerable var-iation in tile surface velocities both in respect of magnitude and direction. If velocities arc to be measured at the surface or at 0-2 depth, it is preferable to avoid heavy wind when it is in or against the direction of flow. At all important sites it is desirable to use all anemometer and record the velocity of wind during the observations.

7.4 Drift, Aquatic Growth - When velocities are measured during floods, care should be exercised to ensure that drift materials such as tree branches do not disturb or damage the current meter and its suspension. Aquatic growth on the channel bottom is also likely to interfere with tile operation of the current meter observation specially when velocities are measured near the bed or at 0�8 depth.

7.4.1 Measurement of Discharges in Weed-infested

Channels-

Wherever possible, effort should be made to a void a weed-infested reach and locate the measuring station elsewhere. Where it is irnpossihie to find allY weed-free site suitable in other respects the method in 7.4.1.1 is likely to yield the best approximation of the flow, btlt not without a larger error than may normally be expected from measurements at a clear site.

8

IS : 3918 � 1966
7.4.1.1 As weeds grow continuously, there is progressively increasing reduction in the effective sectional area and in the velocity and the point of mean velocity along a vertical is also continuously changing. In weed-infested sites, therefore, the point of mean velocity should invariably be determined for each segment of flow during each measuremente Moreover, the number of segments (or verticals) should be relatively larger than in weed-free channels of the same dimensions and discharge. As far as possible, the width of the segment should be fixed on the basis of significant uniformity of weed growth in a segment and the area of the segment scaled down by an appropriate factor based on judgment and experience, for example, tile area of the segment may be taken as 0-9 to 0�95 times tile free area where the weed growth is light, but only 0�75 to 0-8 times the free area where tile weed growth is moderately thick, and so on. In other respect, the normal single-point or surface velocity area method may be used until further research.
NOTE It is recommended that in channels where there are weed .. infested well as clear reaches, research should be carried out by comparative measurements, particularly on tho point of mean velocity 811d the reduction fact.ora to be applied to obtain the area of waterway,

have some effect on reading of the current meter. It may however, be considered negligible for the range of velocities usually measured and for the range of temperature usually met with.

7.6 Effect of Proximity Boundary - It is generally presumed that the cur rent meter rating is affected due to proximity of the boundary, bed and banks of the channel and the free surface.

7.7 Observation at Low Velocity - A cup type current meter suspended from a bobbing boat may be seriously ill error if the velocity is of
the order of 0-3 m/s or less. The cup type current meter should not be used tinder these circumstances.

8. TESTS FOR A CURRENT METER BEFORE USE 8.0 The following tests shall be carried out before and after the day's
observation, a) Spin test, b) Slow motion test, a ltd c) Response to velocity change test.
9

IS : 3918 - 1966

8.1 Spin 'fest - Tile meter shall be rested on a horizontal fiat surface such as a table top and a hard Spill shall be given ttl the bucket wheel by hand, Without spring contact, the spinning time shall be a minimum of 90 sand with spring contact the time shall be a minimum of 75 s.

8.2 Response to Velocity Cbange Test - Immerse the current meter
at 0-6 d and lower it to 0-8 (I; tile change ill number of revolutions of tile bucket-wheel shall be significant in a period of 30 s, even for small changes of velocity of 0-3 tu]� between the two depths. The mean veloci ties to be gauged for the purpose of this test shall be not more than 3 fills or less than O� 5 nl/8.

9. OPERATION AND CARE

10. FAULTS IN REVOLUTION COUNTING
10.1 Wilen the meter is connected to the counter and the bucket wheel revolved, if the counter fails to operate, it may be due to any of the following causes:
�

a) Exhausted batteries, b) Faulty connection to counter, c) Broken electrical connection between instrument and counter, d) Contact breaker failing to make or break circuit) or e) Dirty contacts. 10.2 Test systematically as follows until the fault is located.
a) Switch on the counter and short circuit the two-pin plug at the end of the counter connecting lead. If the short circuit is interrupted the counter should operate. If it does not, the fault lies in the counter connecting lead or the counter itself.

b) Connect the counter to the suspension cable and the cable to the instrument. If the counter fails to operate when the bucket wheel is revolved, hold the two-pin plug at the end of the counter connecting lead against the contact box terminal and the frame of the instrument and again spin the bucket wheel. If the counter now operates there is a fault in the suspension cable or wading rod cables.
13

IS : 3918 - 1966
c) If tile fault lies with the contact breaker in the instrument remove it by unscrewing the knurled ring and determine whether the platinum contacts are pressing together. They may require cleaning with petrol. A drop of thin oil ()11 the contact will prevent short circuiting when gauging in salt water, which is highly conductive, Make sure that tile earth contact at the end of the contact spring is sufficiently protruding to make a good connection to tile tube of the contact box.
d) If adjustment (c) is satisfactory, and the counter still fails when the contact breaker is replaced, tile pin on the bucket spindle may be deflcctillg the contact spring. Remove the contact breaker and adjust t}IC bend in the contact spring so that, when replaced, the circuit is interrupted through 30(l�60� of the rotation of the bucket wheel.

11. FIELD INSTRUCTIONS
11. t A few instructions are necessary for the field operation of the instrument. They may be summarised as follows:

(1) If a suspension cable is being used, take particular care to clamp tile instrument to the suspender rod so that it is ill line
with the sinker weight, and 111(:\ke sure that suspender rod is securely connected to tile cable adapter. b) Attach tile spade con nee tors from the sus pension cable (If the wading rod cable to the met er contact box and earth terminals. I t is advisable to turn t he spade connectors in line with tile

stream flow. c) Ensure that the pivot clamp screw and the contact box clamp
screw have been sufficiently tightened, d) Before lowering the instrument into the water) the bucket wheel should be lowered (")11 t o tile pivot and spur) by hand to ensure that it will spin freely. c) Connect the electric revolution (QUilter or flash counter and eJ1SUre that it registers the rcvolurions precis ely. If thci e is any doubt about the cond it io n of the batteries, replace them by new ones if possible, f) After tile current meter is placed at a selected depth in tile vertical, tile depth being mCaS1JreO to the centre of tile bucket w 11 eel, t h C c u r r e 11t . III e t (~ r s 11 a II IJe pe r 1"1 Jj t ted t o alljus t 10 1he current for a period of half a minute before the reading of tile j nstrurnen t is s tarted, For low velocities of 0�3 fills or less, this time shall be not less than 2 JIlin. After the current meter has adjusted itself tile length of time taken for each reading shall be not less than 40 S making sure

14

IS : 3918 .. 1966
that readings are stopped after tile completion of a full revolution after 40 s or 50 revolutions, whichever is earlier, in order to eliminate tile pulsating effect of the current. g) WIlen observations have been completed for the day, the instrument should be dried to expel water out of tile contact box. Tile pivot shall be dried and oiled before replacing. 11) The bucket wheel shall always be raised from the pivot before replacing the instrument in tile case.
